README.md.text:
# Where to Sell Calculator

One item, every channel. Enter what an item cost you and what you would sell it
for, and see what **eBay, Etsy, Amazon, Mercari, your own store and a direct sale** each
leave you after fees — and after that channel's return rate — plus the price
each channel would need to charge to match the best one, and, when you expect
different volumes on each channel, which one actually keeps more cash in a
month. Then it asks the question a fee table cannot: **how often does it
actually sell there**, and what is one listing worth per month of shelf once
you count that.

**Live tool:** https://duncan-haywood.github.io/monorepo-projects/where-to-sell-calculator/

**Discogs** (records and music media, added 2026-10-19, off by default; its 9% commission on item plus shipping is from Discogs' own fee page and hands the item to [`../discogs-fee-calculator`](../discogs-fee-calculator/); the 2.9% + $0.30 processing default is not a Discogs-published rate and is flagged as such on the page) joins **TCGplayer** (trading cards, added 2026-10-18, off by default; it hands the
item to [`../tcgplayer-fee-calculator`](../tcgplayer-fee-calculator/) for order
size and the Pro schedule, and `channel-parity.test.mjs` checks its profit
against that calculator's one-card order) joins **Walmart Marketplace** (seller-fulfilled, added 2026-10-17, off by default;
it hands the item to [`../walmart-marketplace-calculator`](../walmart-marketplace-calculator/)
for the WFS-versus-ship-it-yourself question, and `channel-parity.test.mjs`
checks its profit against that calculator's seller-fulfilled path) joins
**Depop and Facebook Marketplace** (added 2026-10-16, both off by default; each
opens its dedicated calculator with the item already filled in) join
**Reverb, TikTok Shop, Whatnot, Poshmark and StockX** as more channels,
each switched off until you turn it on. Reverb only applies to musical
instruments and audio gear; Poshmark only to clothing, shoes and accessories;
StockX only to sneakers, streetwear and graded cards; TikTok Shop and Whatnot
only if you sell through those platforms — a channel a seller cannot list on
is noise in a ranking rather than information. None of their fee assumptions
are restated here — `channel-parity.test.mjs` imports them from
[`../reverb-fee-calculator`](../reverb-fee-calculator/),
[`../tiktok-shop-fee-calculator`](../tiktok-shop-fee-calculator/),
[`../whatnot-seller-payout`](../whatnot-seller-payout/),
[`../poshmark-fee-calculator`](../poshmark-fee-calculator/) and
[`../stockx-seller-payout-calculator`](../stockx-seller-payout-calculator/)
and fails if any of the six tools ever quote the same marketplace differently.

### StockX is the one channel where postage is not yours to charge

StockX is a bid/ask marketplace rather than a storefront: the buyer pays
StockX for delivery at checkout, so **no postage a buyer pays ever reaches
the seller**, and the StockX row pins shipping charged to zero rather than
inheriting the shared figure. What the seller *does* pay — the label to a
verification centre — is a real cost and is inherited as normal. Getting this
wrong in the other direction would be expensive rather than untidy: crediting
StockX with postage revenue it never pays out would float it up a ranking the
reader then acts on.

Its seller fee is also the one rate on this page that is genuinely different
per seller — it falls as your own Seller Level rises, and Fast Shipping
enrollment takes more off it again — so the preset is a starting point to
replace with the rate on your own dashboard, and the dedicated calculator is
where the level-versus-Fast-Shipping decision gets made.

### Poshmark is the one channel whose fee is not a rate

Poshmark charges a **flat $2.95 on a sale under $15, and 20% at $15 or more**,
on the item price only. That is a cliff, not a marginal band: the whole sale is
taxed by whichever rule applies. Two consequences the seller can act on, and
neither is visible in a headline-rate table:

- Below **$14.75** — where 20% would have been exactly $2.95 — the flat fee
  costs *more* than the percentage would. A $10 sale pays an effective 29.5%,
  a $5 sale 59%. That is often the worst rate on the whole comparison, and it
  is exactly the price band a closet clear-out lives in.
- Because the switch is at exactly $15.00, the price this page says Poshmark
  needs to reach a target profit can land on either side of it. The solver
  works both branches and returns the one that actually holds, rather than
  dividing by one rate and printing a price the fee schedule does not agree
  with.

This is also why [`../marketplace-fee-compare`](../marketplace-fee-compare/)
leaves Poshmark out and says so on the page: that tool ranks channels by a
single headline rate, and Poshmark does not have one. This page prices a
specific item at a specific price, where the cliff is exactly computable — so
the same fact that disqualifies Poshmark there is what makes it rankable here.

It runs entirely in the browser: static ES modules, no build step, no
dependencies, no server, no account, no API key.

## Why this exists

The single-marketplace calculators in this repo each answer "what does this
order leave me on *this* channel". The question a seller with a listable item
actually asks is "where should I put it", and answering that with three
separate calculators means entering the same costs three times and reconciling
fee structures that are not comparable line by line.

Three things flat "X% fee" comparisons get wrong, all of which this models:

- **Per-listing fees are charged whether or not the item sells.** They dominate
  on cheap items and are invisible in a percentage comparison.
- **A monthly plan is not a per-order cost until it is spread over orders.** At
  10 orders a month a $39 plan is $3.90 an order; at 200 it is 20¢. Comparing
  an own store to a marketplace without that share is the most common error.
- **The fee percentage is not the decision.** What matters is the price each
  channel needs to leave you the same money — a channel with higher fees still
  wins if you can list higher there. That is the last column of the table.
- **A monthly plan needs a volume reality check.** The table shows the minimum
  whole-order count needed for this item's economics to recover a subscription,
  or `—` when no order volume can recover it.
- **Per-sale profit is not monthly cash.** A direct sale that keeps $33 and
  happens four times a month loses to a marketplace that keeps $26 and happens
  forty times. Put expected sales on each channel; a monthly plan is spread
  over that same number so a $39 store plan on 20 sales is $1.95 a sale.
- **A completed sale is not the mix you live in.** A channel that lets you
  list higher can win on every completed order and still lose once you count
  its return rate, return postage, and units that cannot be sold again. The
  table ranks on expected keep after returns unless you turn that overlay off.
- **A sale you never make is worth nothing.** Ranking channels on what they pay
  per sale assumes every channel sells the item. They do not, and the ones that
  sell it slowly charge listing renewals and tie up your cash while they fail
  to. At the shipped defaults Etsy keeps $3.36 more per sale than eBay and is
  worth about a third as much per month of shelf.

## Using it

Open `index.html` in a browser, or serve the directory:

```sh
python3 -m http.server 8000     # then visit /ventures/where-to-sell-calculator/
```

Shared inputs (price, shipping, cost of goods, packaging, expected monthly
orders, plus how long you would leave it listed, what your cash is worth, and
what the item is still worth to you unsold) apply to every channel. Anything a channel does differently — a higher
price on Etsy, no postage on a local sale, an FBA fee on Amazon — goes in that
channel's own panel under the table, along with its rates. Channels can be
switched out of the comparison; "Other channel" starts switched off and blank
for anything not listed (Mercari, Depop, a craft fair, wholesale). Poshmark has
its own row, since the portfolio prices it in depth.

Entries are saved in your own browser so the page remembers them next time.
"Reset everything" clears them.

Use **Copy share link** to send a calculation to someone else. The link carries
only the numeric assumptions and channel settings needed to reproduce the table;
it does not include local usage counts or browser-saved data. Anyone with the
link can read those assumptions, so do not include confidential costs.

Use **Download comparison CSV** to take the ranked table into a spreadsheet.
The file has one row per compared channel and includes fees, keep, expected
keep after returns, monthly keep, days to sell, profit per day, orders to
cover a monthly plan, and the break-even / match-the-leader prices. It is
calculated results only — not your saved usage counts.

### Reading the table

Alongside net profit and margin, each channel reports two figures that answer
questions the ranking alone does not:

- **Break-even price** — how low you can list before the sale costs you money.
  This is the floor for a discount or a "best offer", and it is *different on
  every channel*, because a per-listing fee, a fixed payment fee and a share of
  a monthly plan all have to be recovered before a percentage fee is even
  covered. It turns red when your current price is already below it.
- **Return on cash** — profit against the cash you actually laid out to source,
  pack and ship. Fees come out of the sale rather than your pocket, so they are
  not counted as invested; that keeps the figure comparable across channels
  whose fee structures differ. It reads "—" when nothing was invested (a
  giveaway, or an item with no per-unit cost), rather than an infinite return.
- **Orders to cover plan** — the minimum whole-order volume needed to recover a
  monthly subscription from this item's profit before that plan. It is `0` for
  channels without a monthly plan and `—` when the economics cannot recover it.
- **Monthly keep** — per-sale profit times the sales you expect on that
  channel. Leave the per-channel field blank to use the shared monthly-orders
  figure. When volumes differ, the hero can name a different winner for the
  month than for a single sale.
- **You keep / day** — profit divided by the days you expect that channel to
  take to sell. A no-fee local sale can still lose this comparison if the item
  sits for a month while a marketplace sells next week. Each channel ships with
  an illustrative pace you are expected to replace with how long your last
  similar listings actually took. The column reads "—" when no pace is set,
  rather than inventing one.
- **After returns** — expected keep once some share of orders come back.
  Return postage, unsellable units, and fees the channel does not refund are
  counted on the returned share; a completed sale still keeps the sold profit.
- **Return drag** — the gap between a completed sale and that expected keep.
  It is the number that explains a ranking flip.

Margin answers "how good is this sale", return on cash answers "how hard is my
money working", break-even answers "how far can I move the price", cash
per day answers "do I wait on the cheaper channel or list where it moves",
and after returns answers "does the completed-sale winner still win in the
mix I actually ship".

On a narrow screen the comparison becomes one card per channel instead of a
wide table, with the channel as the card's heading and every figure on its
own labelled line. "Where should I sell this?" is often asked while standing
over the item — at a thrift store, a garage sale, a storage unit — so the
phone layout shows the same numbers rather than a table dragged sideways.

### The second table: what a listing is worth, not what a sale is worth

Everything above ranks a *sale*. A seller with stock is ranking a *listing*,
and a listing only pays out if it sells. The second table ranks the same
channels on that basis:

- **Sells within horizon / days to sell** — your two estimates, per channel.
  These matter more than any fee rate on this page and vary far more by
  category than by channel, so replace them from your own sold-listing history.
- **If it does not** — what a listing costs when it never sells: the
  per-listing fee charged again on every renewal cycle inside your horizon
  (an Etsy listing renews at four months), plus your cash tied up in the item
  for the whole time. Postage, packaging and fulfilment are *not* counted
  here — they are only spent on a sale, and they are already in the figures
  above.
- **One listing is worth** — the two outcomes weighted by sell-through.
- **Per 30 days** — that value spread over the shelf the listing actually
  occupies (shorter when it sells fast). This is what the second ranking uses,
  and it is why a cheaper, faster channel can beat a richer, slower one on the
  same inventory dollar.
- **Sell-through to match** — how often this channel would have to sell to
  earn the leader's rate. Read it as a test of your own estimate: at the
  shipped defaults Etsy needs 72.4% against its assumed 35%, so the ranking
  survives a large error. It reads "—" where no sell-through catches the
  leader.

The two rankings often disagree, and the page says so instead of picking. Take
the higher rate per 30 days when cash or shelf is your constraint; take the
higher keep when you have one item and nothing else the money would be doing.
`does-it-actually-sell-there.html` works one flip through in full.

## Carrying the item into a channel's own calculator

This page answers *which* channel. It does not answer what a promoted listing,
a return, or free shipping then does to that number — the channel's own
calculator in this portfolio does, with twenty-odd scenarios in it.

The gap between those two was retyping. Price, postage, what you paid,
packaging: enter it again or do not go. Most people do not go, so the deeper
tool sits unused and the comparison ends at a ranking nobody acts on.

So under the verdict, every channel that has a dedicated calculator **and** can
accept inputs from a link gets a "keep going with this item" link, built from
what is on screen. Today that is all 16 (`HANDOFFS` in `handoff.mjs`): eBay,
Etsy, Amazon, Mercari, Reverb, TikTok Shop, Whatnot, Poshmark, StockX, Depop,
Grailed, Facebook Marketplace, Walmart, TCGplayer, Discogs and an own store
(Shopify); a channel gains
one the day its calculator learns to read a link.

**The handoff now runs both ways for every channel that has one.** Each of
`../ebay-fee-calculator/`, `../etsy-profit-calculator/`,
`../amazon-fba-calculator/`, `../reverb-fee-calculator/`,
`../shopify-fee-calculator/`, `../tiktok-shop-fee-calculator/`,
`../whatnot-seller-payout/`, `../poshmark-fee-calculator/`,
`../stockx-seller-payout-calculator/`, `../mercari-fee-calculator/`,
`../depop-fee-calculator/`, `../grailed-fee-calculator/`,
`../facebook-marketplace-fee-calculator/`, `../walmart-marketplace-calculator/`,
`../tcgplayer-fee-calculator/` and `../discogs-fee-calculator/`
carries its own item back into this page with
that channel already switched on (each ships its own `to-where-to-sell.mjs`,
mirroring this page's `handoff.mjs` in reverse). Reverb was first; eBay, Etsy,
Amazon and Shopify followed the same day. TikTok Shop and Whatnot followed
later, then Poshmark, StockX on 2026-09-22, and Mercari after that — each
calculator had already exported the field-name
contract this handoff needs (see each one's own `FIELD_IDS` / `INPUT_IDS`), but
none had a where-to-sell channel preset or a `to-where-to-sell.mjs` module
wired up, so a seller who landed on any of those pages first had no way into
this comparison at all, in either direction. Poshmark took longest because it
needed more than wiring: its fee is a cliff rather than a rate, so the ranking
engine had to learn to price, break even and solve for a target on whichever
side of $15 the item sits. This is the direct test of this venture's first
untested hypothesis — until now a seller who searched their way to a
single-channel calculator first (which, for the highest-traffic channels, is
the more likely entry point) had no way into this comparison without
retyping, so the "deeper scenarios never get opened" failure the hypothesis
names could happen from either direction and only one was fixed.

Two details that are not obvious:

- **A channel without a prefillable calculator gets no link at all**, rather
  than a link to a page that would quietly show its own defaults. A wrong
  number that looks like your number is worse than an extra click.
- **A cost the target has no field for is folded in, not dropped.** Etsy has no
  separate packaging input because packaging is part of what it calls
  materials, so packaging is added to `materialCost` on the way over. Dropping
  it would understate cost and overstate profit on arrival.
- **A number the target has no *concept* for is left out, and that is not the
  same thing.** Poshmark's buyer buys a prepaid label at checkout, so postage
  is neither seller revenue nor a seller cost and its calculator has no
  shipping input at all. Folding postage in anywhere would put it inside a
  payout that never sees it, so both shipping fields stay behind — and this
  page's own Poshmark preset starts them at zero for the same reason, so the
  row a seller sees here already agrees with the page they land on.
- **And when the target has no home for a cost that is genuinely real there,
  the right fix is to give it one, not to pick the least-wrong field.** StockX
  resellers pay for a box, tape, a replacement lace bag and label stock, and
  `../stockx-seller-payout-calculator/` had no bucket for any of it — so
  adding the StockX handoff meant adding an `otherCost` input there first.
  The alternative was folding packaging into a field labelled "shipping to
  verification", which preserves the total and prints a line the seller knows
  to be false; a tool that is wrong in a way the reader can see is worse than
  one that is merely incomplete. Its own round-trip test now asserts the net
  profit on the two pages is the same number.

**The link back to the quick triage carries the item too.** The footer link to
`../marketplace-fee-compare/` (headline fees, plus a bulk catalogue view) is rewritten on every
calculation with price, postage, cost and monthly orders, packaging folded into `otherCost`.
Before, it opened empty, so a seller who wanted the shorter view had to retype the item —
the same failure this section exists to remove, in the one direction left. `handoff.test.mjs`
round-trips it through that page's own `decodeShare`.

Nothing is uploaded. The values ride in the URL fragment — the same mechanism
the "Copy share link" button already uses — which browsers never send to a
server, and they only travel inside your own browser as you follow the link.

Field names differ between calculators (`itemCost` here is `costOfGoods` on
eBay and `materialCost` on Etsy), and a name the receiver does not recognise is
*silently dropped* rather than raising an error. `handoff.test.mjs` therefore
imports each target's own field list and fails if a name stops matching, so
that drift breaks a test here instead of a number there.

## A whole inventory at once: the command-line version

Resellers rarely have one item. `cli.mjs` runs a spreadsheet of items through the
same channel presets and the same arithmetic as the page, and prints the best
channel for each item, how far ahead it is of the runner-up, and what routing
every item to its own best channel is worth against listing everything on the
single best channel.

```
node cli.mjs items.csv                       # columns: item, price, cost (or itemCost), shippingCharged, shippingCost, packagingCost, otherCost
node cli.mjs items.csv --also poshmark,depop # add channels that are off by default
node cli.mjs items.csv --channels ebay,etsy  # compare exactly these
node cli.mjs items.csv --csv > routed.csv    # one row per item and channel
node cli.mjs --example                       # try it on invented items
node cli.mjs --list-channels
```

Zero dependencies and no network, so prices and costs never leave the machine. A
fee-free direct sale is left out unless you ask for it with `--also local`,
because it would win every item. The fee and return rates are the page's
illustrative presets, not your account's: treat the output as a ranking to
check, not a forecast. Tests: `cli.test.mjs`.

## Rates are inputs, not a published schedule

Every rate ships with an **illustrative** US default and is editable. This
project does not track, mirror, or assert any marketplace's current fee
schedule — those vary by category, country, plan, and account, and they change.
Replace the defaults with the numbers on your own statements; that is what
makes the comparison yours rather than a generic estimate.

## How fast it sells is part of the answer

The highest net per sale is not the same as the most money per month. A channel
that nets $6 less but sells in three days instead of ninety returns your cash
thirty times more often, and a reseller with finite cash feels that far more
than the six dollars.

So each channel has an optional **days to sell**, and the table shows what it
keeps *per day of waiting* alongside what it keeps per sale. Ranking can be
switched between the two. When they disagree — the usual case once real
turnaround numbers go in — the page says so in words above the table, because
that disagreement is the whole reason to look.

Speed is stated as a **turnover count** ("the same cash goes round 122 times a
year") rather than an annualised percentage. Annualising a three-day flip is
arithmetically true and reads as a promise; the count says the same thing
without implying it compounds.

Each channel ships with an **illustrative** days-to-sell figure, not a claim
about how fast your category actually moves there — how fast a channel moves
*your* category is an observation only you have. Replace it with how long your
last similar listings actually took. Leave it at zero (or blank) for a channel
you have not timed — that reads as unknown, and the channel simply sits out
the speed ranking rather than winning on a blank.

## What it deliberately does not model

Fees are the part that is easy to calculate, not the whole decision. You can
put your own expected sales on each channel so volume can flip the ranking.
Days to sell is your estimate of demand, not a measured marketplace statistic.
Returns and sell-through are inputs, not measurements: this has no way to know
how many buyers a channel puts in front of *you*, or how fast your items
actually move there. Every such rate is a starting point you replace with your
own return report and sold-listing history. A marketplace fee is also partly a
payment for demand you would otherwise have to create. Read the fee, volume,
cash-per-day, return and shelf-time gaps as inputs to the decision, not the
decision.

Also absent: warehouse or storage rent per unit (the FBA-style cost), price
decay on aging stock beyond the single "value you still have if it does not
sell" input, and any interaction between channels — listing the same unit in
two places at once is a real strategy this models as two separate questions.

`returns-change-the-ranking.html` works the Amazon-vs-eBay flip in full;
`does-it-actually-sell-there.html` works the margin-versus-turnover flip.

## Tests

```sh
node --test
```

Covers each channel's fee shape, monthly-plan amortisation (including the
refusal to divide a plan by zero orders), per-channel overrides, break-even and
target-profit solving round-tripping through the calculator, ranking and the
gap against the best channel, per-channel expected volume and the case where
monthly cash ranks a different winner than a single sale, the switched-off-channel
rule, input validation, profit-per-day from expected days to sell (including
the refusal to invent a pace when days are missing), the case where the
fastest channel is not the highest-fee-profit channel, and the usage
counter's opt-out, Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control, and hostile-storage
behaviour.

`handoff.test.mjs` checks the links into the channel calculators, against
each target's *own* field list imported from that venture — so a rename
there fails a test here rather than silently dropping a number there.

`handoff-arrival.check.mjs` is the browser half: it opens each of the 16
target calculators with a handoff link in Chromium and reads the inputs back,
so a target that renames an input id or stops reading the URL fragment fails
there. `handoff-return.check.mjs` does the reverse: it takes each of those 16
calculators' own `to-where-to-sell.mjs` link, opens it here, and checks the
item arrives and that channel's "Compare this channel" box is on. Neither is
part of `node --test` (they need a browser and a local server; usage is in each
file header). Last run 2026-10-19: 16 of 16 in each direction.

`page.test.mjs` adds structural checks on `index.html` itself, because
`calc.test.mjs` imports `calc.mjs` directly and never looks at the page. It
asserts that the results table declares exactly as many columns as the row
template emits cells (a mismatch silently renders every value under the wrong
heading), that every figure named in the page's schema.org `featureList` is
actually rendered, and that the fields which can be `null` are rendered
defensively.

The holding-period tests cover the same ground: that the shipped default
changes no ranking until it is edited, that profit-per-day and turnover divide
by the period, that a blank period reads as unknown rather than instant and
sorts last on speed rather than winning, that a faster channel can outrank a
more profitable one, and that no speed upset is claimed against a channel the
seller never timed.

## Privacy

Everything runs in the visitor's browser. Prices, costs and rates are never
uploaded — there is no server to upload them to. No accounts, cookies, tracking
pixels, or analytics vendors. Saved entries stay in `localStorage` on that
device.

The optional usage counter records only an event name (`comparison_calculated`,
`channel_rates_edited`, `channel_toggled`, `subscription_toggled`,
`channel_volume_edited`, `returns_compared`, `shelf_time_compared`,
`share_link_copied`, `comparison_csv_downloaded`, `handoff_ebay`, `handoff_etsy`,
`handoff_amazon`, `handoff_reverb`, `handoff_own-store`, `handoff_tiktok`,
`handoff_whatnot`, `handoff_poshmark`, `handoff_stockx`, `handoff_mercari`, `handoff_depop`, `handoff_grailed`, `handoff_facebook-marketplace`, `handoff_walmart`, `handoff_tcgplayer`, `handoff_discogs`) and the
current day, in the visitor's own `localStorage`. It never records inputs, it
never leaves the device, it is off for anyone sending Do Not Track or Global
Privacy Control, and the footer checkbox turns it off and discards what was
already counted. It exists so a reading can be reported by hand if a user
volunteers one; there is no collection endpoint.

## Host your own copy

Your data stays in your browser either way, but you can serve the page from an address you control. It is a static
site: the server only hands out files and never sees a figure you type.

- **Phone app:** the page is an installable offline PWA (Chrome "Install app", Safari "Add to Home Screen"), handy for checking an item at a thrift store before buying. `mobile/` packages the same files with Capacitor for Android and iOS builds under your own developer accounts (`mobile/README.md`).
- **Docker:** `docker compose up -d`, then open <http://localhost:8080> (`Dockerfile` is nginx plus the page's files).
- **Fly.io:** `fly launch --copy-config --no-deploy --dockerfile Dockerfile`, then `fly deploy` (`fly.toml`).
- **Render:** deploy from your fork with `render.yaml` (static site, no paid plan needed).
- Nothing runs on the author's accounts. The Docker image has not been built in the session that added these files,
  so build it once and open the page before relying on it. Tests: `node --test deploy.test.mjs`.

does-it-actually-sell-there.html.text:
← Where to Sell Calculator

The channel that pays best is not always the channel to list on

Every fee comparison ranks a sale. A seller with stock is ranking a listing — and a listing only pays out if it sells. Once two channels stop selling the same item equally often, the best-paying channel and the best channel come apart.

The item

A $14 item, $1 to pack, $5 outbound postage, listed at $48 plus $6 shipping on both eBay and Etsy. Illustrative US rates: eBay 13.6% + $0.40 with processing bundled in; Etsy $0.20 a listing, 6.5% transaction, and 3% + $0.25 Etsy Payments. Returns as the returns page models them — 8% on eBay, 4% on Etsy.

On a completed sale, Etsy wins

Illustrative rates. Yours depend on category, plan, and account.
LineeBayEtsy
Order total$54.00$54.00
Fees−$7.74−$5.58
Item, postage, packaging−$20.00−$20.00
Keep on a completed sale$26.26$28.42
Expected keep after returns$23.08$26.71

Etsy’s lower percentage leaves $2.16 more on a completed sale, and its lower return rate widens that to $3.63 once each channel’s returns are counted. Every fee calculator stops here, and on this evidence you list on Etsy.

Now count the listings that do not sell

Say you would leave the item up for 90 days before giving up, your cash is worth 12% a year, and — from your own sold-listing history — listings like this sell inside 90 days about 65% of the time on eBay, taking three weeks, and about 35% of the time on Etsy, taking six and a half weeks. Those are the two numbers to replace with your own; everything below follows from them.

A listing that does not sell is not free. It costs:

  • the per-listing fee again on every renewal — Etsy’s listing expires after four months, so a 90-day run is charged once and a year is charged four times;
  • the cash locked in the item for as long as it sits — $14 at 12% for 90 days is 41¢, small on one item and not small on a hundred;
  • nothing for postage or packaging, which are only spent on a sale.
One listing is worth: sell-through × what a sale keeps + (1 − sell-through) × what sitting costs.
LineeBayEtsy
Sells within 90 days65%35%
Days to sell when it does2145
Worth if it sells$22.99$26.50
Worth if it does not−$0.41−$0.61
One listing is worth$14.80$8.88
Average days on the shelf4574
Per 30 days of shelf$9.83$3.59

Etsy keeps $3.63 more every time the item sells through and is worth about a third as much per month of shelf. The reason is not the fees at all: two Etsy listings in three are still sitting at day 90, tying up cash and earning nothing, while eBay has already turned two in three and freed the money to buy the next item.

How wrong would the estimate have to be?

This is the useful test, because sell-through is the number you are least sure of. Holding everything else fixed, Etsy would need to sell 71.9% of the time inside 90 days — better than double the 35% assumed, and better than eBay’s own rate — to earn as much per month of shelf. If your Etsy history is anywhere near 35%, the ranking is not close, and no plausible error in the fee rates changes it.

Which ranking should you use?

Neither one always. They answer different questions:

  • You are stock-limited — you can source more than you can sell, and cash is the constraint. Take the higher rate per month of shelf; turning the same dollar more often beats a wider margin.
  • You are demand-limited — one item, nothing else to do with the shelf, and no hurry. Take the higher keep. Slow is not a cost when there is nothing else the money or the space would be doing.
  • Both — many sellers list first where it turns and move what has not sold to the higher-margin channel afterwards. The horizon input is exactly that decision: how long before you move it.

What this does not know

Sell-through and time to sale are numbers you supply. Nothing here measures a marketplace, and no default in the calculator is a published or observed rate — they vary more by category than by channel, and yours are in your own sold-listing history. The arithmetic is transparent so you can check it; the inputs are assumptions until you replace them.

Run these numbers on your own item →

Common questions

Should I sell where I make the most per sale or where it sells fastest?

They are different questions. What you keep per sale only pays out if the item sells, so a channel that keeps more per sale but clears one listing in three inside your horizon can be worth less per month of shelf than a cheaper channel that clears two in three quickly. Compare the two directly: weight what you keep by how often listings like yours actually sell, subtract the listing fees charged again on renewal and the cost of the cash tied up while it waits, then divide by the days the listing occupies. If you are stock-limited, take the higher rate per month of shelf. If you are demand-limited and have shelf to spare, take the higher margin.

Does a slow-selling listing cost anything if it never sells?

Yes, in two ways that a fee calculator does not show. Per-listing fees are charged again each time the listing renews, so an Etsy listing that sits for a year is charged four times rather than once. And the money you paid for the item is unavailable for anything else the whole time it sits, which is a real cost whether you would otherwise buy more stock or pay down a card. Postage and packaging are not among the costs — those are only spent when something actually ships.

What sell-through rate should I use?

Your own, from your own sold-listing history, for items like the one you are pricing. Sell-through varies far more by category than by channel: a graded card and a dining table do not share a rate on any marketplace. Any published or default figure is a starting point to replace, not a measurement of your listings. If you have no history, run the comparison at the rate you believe and then at half of it, and see whether the ranking survives being wrong.

etsy-vs-ebay-fees.html.text:
← Where to Sell Calculator

eBay vs Etsy fees on the same item

“Which is cheaper, eBay or Etsy?” has no single answer, because the two fee structures are shaped differently rather than one simply being lower. Here is one item worked through both, with every number visible.

The item

A $48 item with $6 shipping charged to the buyer. It cost $14 to source, $5 to post, and $1 to pack. Same item, same price, same costs — only the channel changes.

eBay

eBay charges a final value fee on the order total, item plus shipping, and that fee normally covers payment processing. On top of it there is a small fixed fee per order. Using an illustrative 13.6% and $0.40:

Illustrative rates. Yours depend on category and account — check a recent statement.
Order total ($48 + $6)$54.00
Final value fee, 13.6% of $54−$7.34
Fixed fee−$0.40
Item, postage, packaging−$20.00
You keep$26.26

Etsy

Etsy splits the same job across four line items: a per-listing fee charged whether or not the item sells, a transaction percentage, and a separate payment-processing percentage and fixed fee. Using an illustrative $0.20, 6.5%, 3% and $0.25:

Illustrative rates. Offsite Ads, when they apply, add another percentage on top.
Order total ($48 + $6)$54.00
Transaction fee, 6.5% of $54−$3.51
Payment processing, 3% of $54 + $0.25−$1.87
Listing fee−$0.20
Item, postage, packaging−$20.00
You keep$28.42

Why the gap moves

On this item Etsy leaves about $2.16 more, because 9.5% in percentage fees plus $0.45 in fixed fees is less than 13.6% plus $0.40. But that gap is not a constant:

  • On cheap items the fixed and per-listing fees dominate. At a $6 sale price, Etsy’s $0.45 of fixed fees plus the listing fee is a far larger share of the order than eBay’s $0.40.
  • Unsold listings only cost money on one side. Etsy’s listing fee is charged whether or not the item sells, so a slow-moving item pays it repeatedly. Model that by raising the per-listing fee to cover the relistings you expect.
  • Offsite Ads can invert the result. When an Etsy sale is attributed to Offsite Ads, an extra percentage lands on the same order total. Put it in the ads field and watch the ranking change.
  • The price you can get is not the same on both. If the same item lists for more on one channel, the fee gap can be irrelevant. That is the question the calculator’s last column answers: the price each channel needs to leave you the same money.

What fees do not tell you

A marketplace fee is partly a payment for demand you did not have to create. A channel that charges 13% and sells the item forty times a month can be worth more than one that charges 9% and sells it four times — and a channel that sells in a week can be worth more than one that sells in three months, because your cash is not sitting in unsold stock. Put those volumes and days-to-sell in each channel’s panel on the calculator — monthly keep and cash per day are the columns that answer that, and a monthly plan is spread over the same volume number. Fees are the part that is easy to calculate, not the whole decision — treat the comparison as one input. Returns are a separate input: a completed-sale winner can lose once each channel’s return rate is counted. Returns can flip the ranking.

Run these numbers on your own item →

Common questions

Is Etsy or eBay cheaper on the same item?

On the worked example of a $48 item with $6 shipping, Etsy leaves about $2.16 more, because 9.5% in percentage fees plus $0.45 in fixed fees is less than eBay's 13.6% plus $0.40. That gap is not a constant: on cheap items the fixed and per-listing fees dominate, Etsy's per-listing fee is charged whether or not the item sells, and Offsite Ads can invert the result.

Do lower marketplace fees mean more profit?

Not on their own. A marketplace fee is partly a payment for demand you did not have to create, so a channel that charges 13% and sells the item forty times a month can be worth more than one that charges 9% and sells it four times. Days to sell and return rates move the ranking too, which is why the calculator compares monthly keep and cash per day rather than fees alone.

index.html.text:
FOR PEOPLE SELLING THE SAME ITEM IN MORE THAN ONE PLACE

One item. Every channel. See where the money actually lands.

Enter what an item cost you and what you would sell it for, once. This compares what eBay, Etsy, Amazon, Mercari, your own store and a direct sale each leave you after their fees — plus Reverb, switched off until you turn it on because it only applies to musical instruments and audio gear — including the per-listing fees and monthly plans that flat “X% fee” comparisons skip — then applies each channel’s return rate so a high-return marketplace cannot win on a completed sale and lose you money in the real mix. When you sell more units on one channel than another, it also ranks expected monthly cash, not just the single sale. It divides what you keep by how many days you expect that channel to take, so a slower no-fee sale does not automatically beat a faster marketplace. Then it asks the question fees alone cannot answer: how often does it actually sell there, and what is one listing worth per month of shelf once you count that. Everything runs in this page; nothing is uploaded.

Already cross-listing everywhere? This tool vs. Vendoo — different jobs, and most resellers want both.

Running inventory across ten-plus marketplaces already? This tool vs. List Perfectly — same split: List Perfectly runs the catalog, this decides where a new item belongs first.

Posting through a browser extension instead? This tool vs. Crosslist — same split: Crosslist posts the listing everywhere, this decides where it belongs first.

Been opening each marketplace’s own fee calculator instead? Here is what that comparison misses — and why you should still check theirs before you price the listing.

Your item

If it does not sell

These apply to every channel. Anything a particular channel does differently — a higher price on Etsy, no postage on a local sale — goes in that channel’s own panel below the table.

Where to sell it

—
$—

Rank by
Same item on every channel, ranked by expected keep after returns unless you turn that overlay off.
Channel Price Fees You keep After returns Return drag Margin Return on cash Gives up Monthly keep Days to sell You keep / day Break-even price Orders to cover plan Price to match best Price for target profit

Break-even price is how low you can list before the sale costs you money — your floor when you discount, and it differs by channel because the fee shapes do. It is shown in red where your current price is already under it. Return on cash is profit against what you actually laid out to source, pack and ship; fees come out of the sale rather than your pocket, so they are not counted as invested. It reads “—” when nothing was invested. Monthly keep is that per-sale profit times the sales you expect on this channel. Leave the per-channel field blank to use the shared monthly-orders figure; fill it in when one channel actually sells more than another. A monthly plan is spread over that same number, so a $39 store plan on 20 sales is $1.95 a sale, not $0.39. You keep / day is what that sale leaves you divided by the days you expect it to take. A no-fee local sale can still lose if the item sits for weeks while a marketplace sells next week. Days are your estimate — the shipped numbers are illustrative starting points, not a marketplace’s sell-through. After returns is the expected keep once some share of orders come back — return postage, units you cannot list again, and fees the channel does not refund. Return drag is the gap between a completed sale and that expected keep. Orders to cover plan is the minimum whole-order volume needed to recover a channel’s monthly subscription from this item’s profit before that plan. “—” means the item’s unit economics cannot recover the plan at any volume; “0” means the channel has no monthly plan.

Transparent arithmetic from the rates you entered — not any marketplace’s current published schedule. Rates vary by category, country, plan and account. Check yours against a recent statement.

Sourcing: the most you can pay for it

Standing at a thrift-store shelf or estate sale? Enter the price you expect to sell for (above) and the profit you want per item. This works backwards through every channel’s fees and your returns overlay and shows the highest purchase price that still gets you there. It ignores what you entered for “what you paid”.

ChannelMost you can pay

And how often does it actually sell there?

—

The same channels ranked on what one listing is worth per 30 days of shelf, not on what one sale is worth.
Channel Sells within horizon Days to sell If it sells If it does not One listing is worth Days on the shelf Per 30 days Gives up Sell-through to match

One listing is worth weights what you keep if it sells against what it costs you if it does not — renewal listing fees for as long as it sits, and your cash tied up in the item meanwhile. Postage, packaging and fulfilment are not double counted here; they are already in the sale figures above and only happen on a sale. Per 30 days divides that by the shelf the listing actually occupies, which is what lets a cheaper, faster channel beat a richer, slower one on the same inventory dollar. Sell-through to match is how often this channel would have to sell to earn the leader’s rate — read it as a test of your own estimate, not a target. A worked example of the flip →

Sell-through and time to sale are the two numbers here you should replace first. They vary more by category than by channel — a graded card and a dining table do not share a sell-through — and the shipped defaults are illustrative, not measured. Your own sold-listing history is the better source.

Each channel’s rates and costs

Opened defaults are illustrative US rates, not a live fee schedule. Replace them with the rates on your own statements — that is what makes the comparison yours rather than a generic estimate.

What this does, and what it does not

Three things flat fee comparisons get wrong

A per-listing fee is charged whether or not the item sells, so it hurts most on cheap items. A monthly plan is only a real per-order cost once you spread it over the orders you actually expect — at ten orders a month a $39 plan is $3.90 an order, at two hundred it is 20¢. The fee percentage is not the decision: what matters is the price each channel needs to leave you the same money, which is the last column above. And the highest profit per sale is not the decision either if one channel sells in a week and another sits for a month — you keep / day is that comparison. eBay vs Etsy fees on the same item works one example through in full, and Reverb vs eBay for selling gear works an $800 guitar through the case where the two answers disagree — the cheaper channel pays more per sale and less per month of shelf. Poshmark vs Mercari vs eBay fees works a $60 jacket through the same split for clothing: the biggest fee leaves the most per sale and the least per month of shelf.

Margin is not the same question as turnover

A fee comparison ranks a sale. A seller with stock ranks a listing. Those come apart the moment two channels do not sell the same item equally often: at the shipped defaults Etsy keeps more per completed sale than eBay and is worth roughly a third as much per month of shelf, because a 35% sell-through leaves most listings still sitting — paying renewal fees and tying up the cash — when eBay has already cleared two in three. The second table ranks that way, and where the two rankings disagree works one example through in full.

What it deliberately leaves out

Fees are not the only difference between channels. A marketplace fee buys you demand you would otherwise have to create. Put your own expected sales in each channel’s panel to see when volume flips the ranking. Days-to-sell is your estimate of that demand, not a measured sell-through rate, and the page still has no way to know how many buyers each channel puts in front of you — sell-through and time to sale are numbers you supply, not measurements. Returns are an input the same way: each channel has a rate, return postage, a still-sellable share, and a fee-refund share you can replace with your own report. Returns can flip the ranking works one Amazon-vs-eBay example through in full. Read the fee, volume, cash-per-day, return and shelf-time gaps as inputs to the decision, not the decision. It does not recommend a price, a channel, or a business model, and it is not tax, financial or business advice.

Common questions

Is it cheaper to sell on eBay or Etsy?

It depends on the item, because the two fee shapes are different rather than one simply being lower. eBay charges a percentage of the order total that normally includes payment processing, plus a small fixed fee. Etsy charges a per-listing fee whether or not the item sells, a transaction percentage, and a separate payment-processing percentage and fixed fee. On a low-priced item the per-listing and fixed fees matter most; on a high-priced item the percentages dominate. Enter your own numbers above — this page does no more than the arithmetic on the rates you give it.

How do I compare marketplace fees fairly?

Put the same item through every channel with the same cost of goods, then make three adjustments most comparisons skip. Spread any monthly subscription over the orders you actually expect that month. Count per-listing fees, which are charged whether or not the item sells. And compare the price each channel needs to reach the same profit, not just the fee percentage, because a channel with higher fees can still win if you can list higher there.

Does selling on my own store beat a marketplace?

On fees alone an own store usually wins, because there is no marketplace commission — only card processing and the monthly plan spread over your orders. What it does not include is the buyers. Put the number of sales you actually expect on each channel in that channel's panel: a store that keeps more per sale can still lose the month to a marketplace that sells more units. The honest comparison is the fee gap against the volume each channel can carry.

Should I sell on the cheapest channel or the fastest one?

A channel that keeps more per sale can still lose if the item sits longer. Divide what you keep by how many days you expect that channel to take to sell, and compare cash per day — not just cash per sale. The days are your estimate, not a marketplace statistic. Replace the illustrative starting points with how long your last similar listings actually took.

Do marketplace returns change which channel is cheapest?

They can. A completed sale on Amazon can look better than eBay once you list a few dollars higher, then lose once you count Amazon's higher return rate, return postage, and units that cannot be sold again. This page ranks channels on expected keep after the return rate you enter — turn that overlay off to see the sold-sale ranking only. Rates are inputs, not a published marketplace schedule.

Should I sell where I make the most per sale or where it sells fastest?

Those are two different questions and they often have different answers. What you keep per sale only matters if the item sells; a channel that pays more but clears one listing in three inside your horizon can be worth less per month of shelf than a cheaper channel that clears two in three quickly. This page ranks both ways side by side: what you keep if it sells, and what one listing is worth per 30 days of shelf once you count sell-through, time to sale, listing fees charged again on renewal, and the cash tied up while it waits. Where the two rankings disagree you are choosing between margin and turnover, and the tool says so rather than picking for you.

How do I work out what a listing is worth per month?

Take what you keep if it sells, subtract any listing fee charged again while it waits and the cost of the cash tied up in the item, and weight that by how often listings like it actually sell inside the period you would leave it up. The listings that do not sell still cost renewal fees and carry. Divide the result by the average days the listing occupies — shorter when it sells quickly — and multiply by thirty. That per-month figure, not the fee percentage, is what compares a fast channel against a rich one on the same inventory dollar.

# Where to Sell Calculator as an Android and iOS app

The web app is already installable: open it in Chrome (Install app) or Safari
(Share, Add to Home Screen) and it runs full screen and offline from a service
worker. This folder is for people who want a store build of their own.

The calculator is plain HTML and ES modules with no bundler, so
[Capacitor](https://capacitorjs.com/) wraps it unchanged.

```bash
cd ventures/where-to-sell-calculator/mobile
npm install
# Set your own appId in capacitor.config.json first (reverse-domain, e.g. com.yourco.wheretosell).
npm run add:android     # needs Android Studio
npm run add:ios         # needs macOS and Xcode
npm run open:android    # build, sign and upload with YOUR developer account
```

Rebuild after changing the calculator: `npm run sync-web && npx cap sync`.

Publishing to Google Play or the App Store happens under your own developer
account and your own appId. Nothing here signs, uploads or runs on anyone's
behalf. The app makes no network calls; the figures stay on the device.

← Where to Sell Calculator

Returns can flip where the money actually lands

Fee comparisons rank a completed sale. Sellers do not live in that world. A channel that lets you list higher can still lose once you count the share of orders that come back, the return postage you pay, and the units that cannot be sold again.

The item

Same source cost on both channels: $14 to buy, $5 outbound postage, $1 to pack. eBay lists at $48 plus $6 shipping. Amazon lists at $54 plus the same $6 — a realistic Prime premium, not a different product.

Completed sale: Amazon wins

Using illustrative US rates — eBay 13.6% + $0.40, Amazon 15% referral plus $39.99/month spread over 100 orders — the completed sales look like this:

Illustrative rates. Yours depend on category, plan, and account.
LineeBay at $48Amazon at $54
Order total$54.00$60.00
Percentage and plan fees−$7.74−$9.40
Item, postage, packaging−$20.00−$20.00
You keep on a completed sale$26.26$30.60

List $6 higher on Amazon and the completed sale leaves about $4 more. That is the ranking a fee-only calculator reports.

After returns: eBay wins

Now apply illustrative return assumptions a seller can replace with their own report: eBay 8% of orders come back, Amazon 18%. Return postage is $6 on eBay and $7 on Amazon. Nine in ten eBay returns can be listed again; four in five Amazon returns can. Percentage fees are refunded; the Amazon plan share is not.

Expected keep = (1 − return rate) × sold profit + return rate × cash on a returned order.
LineeBayAmazon
Cash on a returned order−$13.40−$16.20
Return rate8%18%
Expected keep$23.08$22.18
Return drag versus a perfect sale$3.17$8.42

Amazon still looks better on every completed sale. In the mix a seller actually lives in, eBay leaves $0.90 more. The $4 completed-sale gap was more than eaten by the extra returns.

What the calculator counts on a return

  • You refund the buyer, so there is no sale revenue.
  • Outbound postage, packaging, and fulfilment are already spent.
  • You pay return postage unless you set it to zero (buyer-paid returns).
  • A share of percentage and fixed payment fees may come back; listing fees and the monthly-plan share do not.
  • Units that cannot be sold again cost you the item. Units that can are inventory again, not a second purchase.

None of those rates is a published marketplace schedule. Replace them with the numbers on your own return report — apparel often comes back more often than hard goods, and “still sellable” is the assumption that moves the ranking most after the return rate itself.

Can returns change which marketplace is more profitable?

Yes. In the worked example Amazon keeps $30.60 on a completed sale against eBay's $26.26, but at an 8% eBay return rate and an 18% Amazon return rate the expected keep is $23.08 on eBay and $22.18 on Amazon. The $4 completed-sale lead is more than eaten by the extra returns.

What does a returned order actually cost a seller?

You refund the buyer, so there is no sale revenue, and outbound postage, packaging, and fulfilment are already spent. You pay return postage unless the buyer does. A share of percentage and fixed payment fees may come back, but listing fees and the monthly-plan share do not. Units that cannot be sold again cost you the item, and units that can are inventory again rather than a second purchase.

← Where to Sell Calculator

Reverb vs eBay for selling gear

Reverb charges roughly a third of what eBay does on the same guitar, and the cheaper channel is still not automatically the right one. Here is one instrument worked through both, with every number visible and nothing hidden in a headline percentage.

The item

An $800 guitar with $75 shipping charged to the buyer. It cost $450 to acquire, $65 to ship, and $20 to pack properly — a case, foam, and a double box, because gear that arrives with a cracked headstock is a claim, not a sale. Same instrument, same price, same costs. Only the channel changes.

Fee by fee

Illustrative rates, not published schedules. Both are inputs you can change on the calculator.
On $875 collectedReverbeBay
Selling / final value fee$40.00 (5% of item)$119.00 (13.6%)
Payment processing$28.40 (3.19% + $0.49)$0.40 (inside the fee above)
Total fees$68.40$119.40
Profit if it sells$271.60$220.60
Margin31.0%25.6%

The structural difference is worth understanding, because it is why the gap is not simply “5% against 13.6%”. eBay’s final value fee normally has payment processing folded into it and runs on the whole order, so the one percentage is most of the bill. Reverb bills the selling fee on the item price only and the processor separately on the order, so the 5% headline is not the whole cost — the real comparison here is 5% of the item plus 3.19% of the order and $0.49, against 13.6% of the order. Still a large gap on this item: about $51 more in your pocket on Reverb.

Then returns, which move it slightly

Gear buyers inspect on arrival and return postage on an instrument is not $6. Counting an illustrative 6% return rate on Reverb against 8% on eBay, and the heavier return shipping that gear carries, the expected keep across a run of sales is $246.42 on Reverb against $192.07 on eBay — a $54.35 gap, slightly wider than the single-sale one. Returns do not flip this comparison. They can flip others: see how.

And then the thing that does flip it

Illustrative days to sell — replace these with how long your own listings actually take.
ReverbeBay
Days to sell3521
Kept per day of wait$7.76$10.50
Worth per 30 days of shelf$59.14$82.95

Reverb pays more per sale. eBay pays more per month of shelf. The cheaper channel loses on the measure that matters when your money is the constraint, because a slower sale ties up $535 of cash for another two weeks and that capital could have been another instrument. Which column you should read depends on which one you are short of:

  • Short of cash — you flip gear, and the money in this guitar is the money for the next one. Read cash per day. The faster channel can be worth more even while charging more in fees.
  • Short of gear — this is a personal instrument, or stock you are not replacing this month. Nothing is waiting on the money, so read profit per sale, and the fee gap is the whole story.

There is a third answer the arithmetic cannot give you: gear buyers on Reverb arrive already looking for gear. Whether that audience will carry a higher price is a judgement about your particular instrument. What the calculator can tell you is the size of the premium you would need — eBay would have to sell this guitar for about $868, roughly 8.5% more, to leave what Reverb leaves at $800.

Run it on your own instrument

Every figure above is the calculator’s own arithmetic on the inputs named, not a published fee schedule, and the days-to-sell numbers are illustrative starting points rather than a claim about either marketplace’s velocity. Your acquisition cost, your shipping, and your own listing history are what make the comparison mean anything.

Put your own instrument through both → Reverb is switched off by default there, since most sellers are not selling gear — turn it on in the channel list. Once you have an answer, the comparison hands the same numbers to the Reverb calculator, which asks the questions this page cannot: whether to take an offer or counter it, whether a bump pays for itself, whether Safe Shipping beats carrying the claim risk yourself, and what consigning to a shop would actually net.

Common questions

Is Reverb or eBay cheaper for selling a guitar?

On the worked example of an $800 guitar with $75 shipping charged, Reverb's fees come to $68.40 against eBay's $119.40, so Reverb leaves about $51 more on the sale. Reverb bills a 5% selling fee on the item price and payment processing separately on the order; eBay charges around 13.6% on the order with processing already inside it. The gap narrows on cheaper items where the fixed fee matters more, and both rates are inputs you should replace with your own.

Does Reverb being cheaper mean I should list there?

Not on its own. In the same worked example eBay returns $10.50 per day against Reverb's $7.76, because the illustrative 21 days to sell on eBay beats 35 on Reverb. Cheaper fees on a slower sale can be worth less per month of shelf than higher fees on a faster one. If your cash is the constraint, the faster channel can win even while paying more in fees; if the gear is not going anywhere, the cheaper channel wins.

How much more would eBay have to sell for to match Reverb?

About $864 on this example, against the $800 asked on Reverb — roughly 8.5% more, because eBay's percentage fee applies to the higher price too. Whether a listing can carry that premium is a judgement about the buyers on each side, not arithmetic, which is why the calculator prints the price to match rather than picking for you.

vs-crosslist.html.text:
← Where to Sell Calculator

This tool vs. Crosslist

Two different jobs in the same reseller's workflow. Crosslist posts one listing to every marketplace you connect it to. This page decides which marketplace is worth listing on in the first place — free, in your browser, before anything gets posted anywhere.

What each product is for

Crosslist is a paid subscription browser extension for resellers. You create one listing — photos, description, price — and it posts that same listing across the marketplaces you connect: eBay, Poshmark, Mercari, Depop, Facebook Marketplace, and others. Its features are built around posting speed and reach: bulk crosslisting, relisting, and automation like sold-item detection and auto-delist so a sold item does not stay listed (and returnable) elsewhere. It is built for a reseller who has already decided an item is going up everywhere and wants that to take seconds instead of an hour of retyping.

This page does none of that. It creates nothing, posts nothing, and connects to no marketplace account. It takes one item you are still deciding about — price, cost, expected volume, expected days to sell, return rate — and ranks the net profit eBay, Etsy, Amazon, your own store and a direct sale would each leave you, both per sale and per day of waiting. Its subject matter is the decision that comes before a listing exists: is this even worth posting everywhere, or does one or two channels clearly win and the rest just cost renewal fees and shelf time for nothing back.

What you want to knowWhere to answer it
I have decided to list this everywhere — how do I get it posted to five marketplaces without retyping it five times?Crosslist or a comparable cross-listing app — that is the job it is built for.
I am holding one item and have not listed it anywhere yet. Which channel actually nets me the most?This tool — type it once, see every channel ranked by profit, free and instantly.
An item sold on one marketplace — can it be pulled from the others automatically?Crosslist — auto-delist is one of its features; this page has no connection to any marketplace to do that.
Is it worth listing this on all five channels, or would three of them just tie up cash and pay renewal fees for nothing?This tool — it ranks channels on expected keep after returns and value per month of shelf, so a channel not worth listing on shows up as one.
At what price does this item break even on each channel?This tool — it prints a per-channel break-even price from the cost you typed.
Do I have to connect a marketplace account, or pay a subscription, to use it?This tool: no, and never will. Crosslist connects to your marketplace accounts by design, because posting a listing is the job it does.

A reseller can reasonably use both, in sequence: this page to decide where an item is worth listing, then Crosslist (or another cross-lister, or listing by hand) to actually get it posted there. They are not competing answers to one question. This page makes no claim about Crosslist's accuracy, features, or current terms, and does not evaluate it — it describes only the shape of the product, as Crosslist describes it publicly, and states what this tool does differently.

No account and no sign-in: this is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

What this tool cannot tell you

Worth being blunt about, because it is the honest half of the comparison above. This page never touches a real marketplace account, so it cannot do what Crosslist does:

  • It does not create, edit, or post a listing anywhere. No photos, no description, no publish button. It only ranks the arithmetic of channels you have not listed on yet.
  • It has no idea when an item sells. It cannot delist a sold item from other channels the way Crosslist's automation does — it has nothing connected to delist from.
  • The fee rates are editable defaults, not a live fee schedule. They were current when the page was written. Marketplaces change them. Confirm against your own statement before pricing a catalogue.
  • Days to sell and return rate are your estimates, not measurements. The page has no order history for any channel; replace the illustrative defaults with your own sold-listing history for a ranking worth trusting.

Those limits are the reason the comparison above is a comparison of shapes rather than a claim that one product replaces the other.

Common questions

Should I use this tool or Crosslist?

They answer different questions, and most resellers who use one eventually want the other. Crosslist is a paid subscription browser extension that posts one listing to the marketplaces you connect — eBay, Poshmark, Mercari, Depop, Facebook Marketplace and others — with bulk crosslisting, automatic delisting when an item sells elsewhere, and relisting tools. It assumes you have already decided to list an item everywhere and answers "how do I do that fast". This page assumes nothing has been listed yet and answers "which of eBay, Etsy, Amazon, my own store or a direct sale would actually net me the most on this specific item", ranked by profit after fees and returns, and by profit per day once you count how long each channel takes to sell. It has no account, connects to no marketplace, and posts nothing anywhere.

Can this page replace Crosslist?

No, and it is not trying to. This page never creates or posts a listing. It takes the price, cost and fee assumptions you type and ranks the arithmetic across channels — it cannot photograph your item, write a description, or push a listing live anywhere, which is the job Crosslist is built for. Once this page has told you which one or two channels are worth listing on, Crosslist (or listing by hand) is how the item actually gets posted.

Does Crosslist tell me which marketplace is most profitable?

Not as its primary job. Crosslist's own description centers on posting speed and reach across connected marketplaces — plus automation like sold-item detection and auto-delist once an item sells elsewhere — rather than modelling each marketplace's fee structure, return rate, and sell-through against your item's cost and price to rank net profit. This page does only that one calculation, and does not create, edit, or post a listing anywhere.

Is this page affiliated with Crosslist?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Crosslist. Crosslist is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this tool is and is not, based on Crosslist's own public description of its product.

Open the where to sell calculator to rank your own item, or read a worked example of margin vs. turnover for the case where the two rankings disagree.

vs-each-marketplaces-own-calculator.html.text:
← Where to Sell Calculator

This tool vs. each marketplace’s own fee calculator

Every marketplace publishes a calculator for its own fees, and on its own fees each one is the authority. None of them can tell you where to list, because none of them has a figure for what the other channels would have paid. That comparison is the job of this page — free, in your browser, before the item is listed anywhere.

What each one is for

A marketplace’s own calculator answers one question completely: what will selling this item here cost me? It is maintained by the company that sets the fees, it reflects the schedule currently published, and it usually knows the category-specific rates and the account-level details — a store subscription tier, a promotion — that a third party cannot see. On its own channel it should be treated as the authority, and this page does not compete with it.

What it cannot do is rank. It has no figure for what a different channel would have paid, and no reason to produce one. So a seller holding one unlisted item opens three calculators, writes three numbers down, and compares them — and that reconciliation step, not the fee arithmetic inside any of the three, is where the answer goes wrong.

What you want to knowWhere to answer it
I have decided to list on this one marketplace. Exactly what will its fees be on my account, in my category?That marketplace’s own calculator — it is the authority on its own schedule, and this page is not.
I am holding one item and have not listed it anywhere. Which channel leaves me the most?This tool — type the item once and every channel is ranked side by side on the same fee base.
Channel A pays more per sale but Channel B sells in half the time. Which should get the listing?This tool — it ranks on profit per day of wait and on what a listing is worth per month of shelf, not only on profit per sale.
Is a channel with a flat monthly plan worth it at the volume I actually do?This tool — it spreads a monthly cost over the orders you expect, so the plan stops looking like a per-sale fee.
Do returns change the ranking?This tool — it models per-channel return rate, who pays return postage, how much fee comes back, and how often the item is resellable.
What price would this channel need to match the best one?This tool — it prints the matching price and the break-even price per channel.
Do I need an account, a subscription, or a sign-in?This tool: none of the three. It is a static page and the arithmetic runs in your browser.

Four things that go wrong when you reconcile them by hand

These are the reasons a page like this exists at all. Each one is a difference between channels that a single-channel calculator has no occasion to mention, because within its own channel it is a constant.

1. The headline percentages are not the same kind of number

Marketplaces bundle their fees differently. On some, the selling commission already covers payment processing, so the single percentage you see is the whole story. On others, processing is billed separately as its own percentage plus a fixed amount per order, and a third charge applies per listing whether or not the item ever sells. Subtracting one headline rate from another therefore compares two quantities that do not contain the same things, and the gap it reports is not the gap in what you keep. This page puts every channel through one model — commission, processing, per-listing and monthly costs as separate inputs — so what is compared at the end is net, not headline.

2. A monthly plan is not a per-sale fee

A flat monthly subscription does not change with the sale, so it cannot be expressed as a percentage of one order without knowing how many orders the month will hold. At one sale a month it is the largest cost on the item; at fifty it rounds to nothing. A per-item calculator has no volume to spread it over and either omits it or attributes the whole month to the one item on screen. This page asks for expected monthly volume and amortises the plan across it, which is the only way that cost is comparable to a percentage on a rival channel.

3. Returns are not symmetrical between channels

Channels differ in how often items come back, who ends up paying the return postage, how much of the original fee is refunded to the seller, and how often a returned item can be sold again rather than written down. Those four together decide what you expect to keep, which can rank channels differently from what you are paid on a sale that sticks. A single-channel calculator has no cross-channel comparison to make, so it reports the clean sale. This page reports both, and the ranking after returns is the one it leads with.

4. A listing occupies shelf time, and shelf time is finite

The channel that pays most per sale is not always the channel to list on. If it takes twice as long to sell, the same cash and the same item are tied up twice as long, and a slower channel may also renew the listing — and charge for it again — before the item moves. For a seller with finite stock and finite cash the question is closer to return per month of shelf than profit per sale. No marketplace’s own calculator models this, because the alternative use of the shelf is always another marketplace. This page ranks on it explicitly, and says so when the two rankings disagree.

The sell-through and days-to-sell figures it starts with are illustrative defaults, not measurements of how fast any marketplace sells. Replace them with your own sold-listing history before trusting the shelf-time ranking — that is the input it is most sensitive to.

What the marketplaces’ own calculators do better

The honest half of the comparison. On the question they are built for, they beat this page, and a seller who uses only this one is missing things:

  • They are the current schedule; this page is not. The rates here are editable defaults that were accurate when the page was written, and they are inputs rather than a published fee schedule. Marketplaces change fees. The marketplace’s own calculator changes with them on the day.
  • They know your category. Referral and final-value rates commonly vary by category, and some categories carry exceptions and caps. This page uses one rate per channel — the one you type.
  • They know your account. A store subscription tier, a promotional period, a seller-level discount, a regional difference: all of that is visible to the marketplace and invisible here.
  • They can see your real orders. Some are wired into your actual listings and settlement reports. This page has no account, no connection, and no order history — every figure in it is one you supplied.

So the sequence that gets the most out of both is: rank the channels here while the item is still unlisted, then confirm on the winning channel’s own calculator with your own account’s rates before you set the price. This page makes no claim about any marketplace calculator’s accuracy or current terms, and does not evaluate one — it describes only the shape of what each kind of tool is for.

No account and no sign-in: this is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off. Nothing you type is uploaded.

Common questions

Why not just use each marketplace's own fee calculator?

Because each one is scoped to a single marketplace, and the question you are actually asking spans several. A marketplace calculator answers "what will selling this here cost me" accurately and from its own published schedule. It cannot answer "should I sell it here", because it has no figure for what any other channel would have paid, and no reason to produce one. To turn three correct single-channel answers into a ranking you have to reconcile them yourself, and that reconciliation — not the fee arithmetic — is where the mistakes happen.

What goes wrong when I compare marketplace calculators by hand?

Four things, and each one is easy to miss. The fee bases differ: one marketplace's commission already includes payment processing while another bills processing separately, so the headline percentages are not the same kind of number and cannot be subtracted from each other. Fixed monthly costs are not per-sale costs, so a subscription only makes sense spread over the orders you actually expect that month. Returns are not symmetrical — channels differ in how often items come back, who pays the return postage, how much of the fee is refunded, and whether the item can be sold again. And a listing occupies shelf time: a channel that pays more per sale but takes twice as long to sell it can be the worse place to put finite cash.

Is this page more accurate than the marketplace's own calculator?

No, and on its own fees a marketplace's calculator should be treated as the authority. It is maintained by the company that sets the fees, it reflects the current published schedule, it knows category-specific rates, and it can account for whatever your own account is actually charged — a store subscription tier, a promotion, a category exception. This page's rates are editable defaults that were current when it was written, and they are inputs rather than a fee schedule. What this page adds is not precision on one channel; it is one consistent comparison across all of them.
